Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.description:

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always skipped for safety, even when `include_ignored` is `true`.

Matched against each file's full absolute path, so a path-anchored pattern like `src/**/*.ts` silently matches nothing — use a basename pattern (`*.ts`), or anchor with `**/` (`**/src/**/*.ts`). To scope the search to a directory, use `path` instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Read a text file from the local filesystem.

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). Use `Grep` only when the task is to search for unknown content or locations.

When you need several files, prefer to read them in parallel: emit multiple `Read` calls in a single response instead of reading one file per turn.

- Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.
- Returns up to 1000 lines or 100 KB per call, whichever comes first; lines longer than 2000 chars are truncated mid-line.
- Page larger files with `line_offset` (1-based start line) and `n_lines`. Omit `n_lines` to read up to the 1000-line cap.
- Sensitive files (`.env` files, credential stores, SSH private keys, and similar secrets) are refused to protect secrets; do not attempt to read them. Templates and public keys are exempt: `.env.example` / `.env.sample` / `.env.template` and public SSH keys such as `id_rsa.pub` read normally.
- Only UTF-8 text files can be read. Non-UTF-8 encodings, binary files, and files containing NUL bytes are refused; use `ReadMediaFile` for images or video, and Bash or an MCP tool for other binary formats.
- Negative line_offset reads from the end of the file (for example, -100 reads the last 100 lines); the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.
- Output format: `<line-number>\t<content>` per line.
- A `<system>...</system>` status block is appended after the file content; it summarizes how much was read (line and byte counts, truncation, line-ending notes) and is not part of the file itself.
- Pure CRLF files are displayed with LF line endings; `Edit` matches this output and preserves CRLF when writing back.
- Mixed or lone carriage-return line endings are shown as `\r` and require exact `Edit.old_string` escapes.
- After a successful `Edit`/`Write`, do not re-read solely to prove the write landed. When the task depends on an exact file, API, or output shape, inspect the final external contract before finishing.

path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

`HOME=/tmp/nshprobe ./executable --norc -c '...'`, stdout/stderr captured separately).

- `$$`, `$!`, and all PIDs/addresses in Rust panic backtraces are nondeterministic.
- Panic backtraces (full `nsh:    0: 0x...` frames) are printed on stderr after the panic

=====================================================================
## 1. Basic parameter expansion: $VAR, ${VAR}
=====================================================================

`x=hello; echo $x`      → stdout `hello\n`, exit 0
`x=hello; echo ${x}`    → stdout `hello\n`, exit 0
`echo $UNSET_VAR`       → stdout `\n` (empty line), exit 0   (unset → empty string, no error)

CRITICAL non-POSIX behavior — field splitting at expansion boundaries:
An unquoted parameter expansion is ALWAYS split out into its own field(s), separate from
adjacent literal text in the same word. Quoted expansion concatenates normally.

`x=hi; echo ${x}y`      → stdout `hi y\n`        (two fields: "hi", "y"; echo joins with space)
`x=hi; echo "${x}y"`    → stdout `hiy\n`
`echo $HOME/x`          → stdout `/tmp/nshprobe /x\n`   (fields "/tmp/nshprobe" and "/x")
`x=""; printf '<%s>\n' pre${x}post` → stdout:

`printf '<%s>\n' $UNSET`        → stdout `<>\n`   (ONE empty field — empty expansions are NOT removed)
`printf '<%s>\n' ${UNSET}${UNSET}` → stdout `<>\n<>\n` (two empty fields)

`printf '<%s>\n' $(printf "a b\tc\nd")` → `<a>` `<b>` `<c>` `<d>`
`printf '<%s>\n' $(printf "a\n\nb")`    → `<a>` `<>` `<b>`   (interior empty line → empty field)
`printf '<%s>\n' pre$(printf "a\nb")post` → `<pre>` `<a>` `<b>` `<post>` (boundary splitting, like §1)
`printf '<%s>\n' $(echo "  spaced  ")`  → `<>` `<>` `<spaced>` `<>` `<>`
`x=$(echo a)$(echo b); printf '%s' "$x" | od -c` → bytes `a b` ("ab"; adjacent substs concatenate)
`echo a$(echo)b` → `a  b`  (fields "a","","b" joined by echo's spaces — empty subst yields an empty field)

EMPTY substitutions: `echo $( )` → empty line, no error; `echo $()` → empty line, no error.

REDIRECTS inside work: `echo $(echo hi >/tmp/csout); cat /tmp/csout` → stdout `\nhi\n`
(the echo inside wrote to the file; the substitution captured nothing).

EXIT STATUS IS NOT PROPAGATED (non-POSIX):
`x=$(false); echo $?`      → `0`
`x=$(exit 3); echo $?`     → `0`
`x=$(nosuchcmd); echo $?`  → `0` (stderr still gets `nsh: command not found \`nosuchcmd'`)
`echo $(echo x; exit 3); echo "st=$?"` → `x` / `st=0` (echo's status wins, as in POSIX)
Assignments inside the substitution do not leak:
`x=before; echo $(x=after); echo "parent x=$x"` → empty line / `parent x=before`
`y=$(x=after; echo $x); echo "y=$y x=$x"`       → `y=after x=`

- Backslash does NOT escape a backtick inside backticks (no nesting via \`):

- Backticks containing $(...) work: `echo \`echo $(echo x)\`` → `x`.
- Multi-line output in backticks splits the same way: `echo \`echo a; echo b\`` → `a b`.

PROCESS SUBSTITUTION (grammar supports it):
`cat <(echo hi)`   → `hi`   (works)
`echo hi >(cat)`   → PANIC, exit 101; stderr:

## 7. Tilde expansion
=====================================================================

`echo ~`        → `/tmp/nshprobe`      ($HOME — captured at shell STARTUP; `unset HOME; echo ~`
                                        still prints the original HOME)
`echo ~/x`      → `/tmp/nshprobe/x`
`echo "~"` / `echo '~'` → `~`          (quoted: no expansion)
`echo a~`       → `a~`                 (only at word start or after `=`)
`echo a=b~`     → `a=b~`
`echo a=~`      → `a=/tmp/nshprobe`    (tilde after `=` expands, even in a non-assignment word)
Assignment context: `x=~/bin; echo $x` → `/tmp/nshprobe/bin`; `export A=~/b; echo $A` → `/tmp/nshprobe/b`
`x=a:~; echo $x` → `a:~`               (tilde after `:` does NOT expand)

`~user`, `~+`, `~-` are ALL unsupported. Each prints to stderr:
    nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported
(the literal text is always `~user` regardless of what followed the tilde) and the tilde-span
—which consumes everything up to the next `/`—expands to $HOME. Exit code stays 0.
`echo ~root`     → `/tmp/nshprobe` + warning
`echo ~nouser`   → `/tmp/nshprobe` + warning
`echo ~+`        → `/tmp/nshprobe` + warning
`echo ~-`        → `/tmp/nshprobe` + warning   (even after `cd /tmp`, `~-` is HOME, not OLDPWD)
`echo ~root/x`   → `/tmp/nshprobe/x` + warning
`x=~:~/bin; echo $x` → `/tmp/nshprobe/bin` + ONE warning
    (the span `~:~` is ONE tilde expansion of "user" `:~` → HOME, then literal `/bin`)
`echo x=~:~`     → `x=/tmp/nshprobe` + warning (same: span `~:~` after `=`)

=====================================================================
## 8. Field splitting (IFS)
=====================================================================

Applies to UNQUOTED expansion results only. Rules observed:
- Splits on EACH IFS character occurrence individually; NO collapsing of adjacent separators;
  every separator produces a field boundary, so empty fields are preserved everywhere
  (leading, middle, trailing).
- Default IFS is unset (`echo "IFS=[$IFS]"` → `IFS=[]`) but splitting still happens on
  space, tab, and newline (inferred default; tab/newline splitting directly observed for
  command-substitution output).
- Additionally, every expansion in a word forms its own field group, separate from adjacent
  literal text (see §1): `pre${x}post` with x=" a  b " yields fields from the literals and
  the split value concatenated: e.g. x="  pad  ": `printf '<%s>\n' z${x}z` →
  `<z>` `<>` `<>` `<pad>` `<>` `<>` `<z>` (7 fields).
- Empty expansion → exactly one empty field (never deleted).
- Quoted expansions never split.
- Expansion RESULTS ARE NEVER GLOBBED (see §9).

`v=" a  b "; printf '<%s>\n' $v`     → `<>` `<a>` `<>` `<b>` `<>`     (5 fields!)
`x="a b"; printf '<%s>\n' $x`        → `<a>` `<b>`
`x="a b"; printf '<%s>\n' "$x"`      → `<a b>`
`IFS=x; v="aXbxc"; printf '<%s>\n' $v` → `<aXb>` `<c>`    (splits only on lowercase x)
`IFS=,; v="a,b,,c"; printf '<%s>\n' $v` → `<a>` `<b>` `<>` `<c>`  (empty field from `,,`)
`IFS=" ,"; v="a, b,c"; printf '<%s>\n' $v` → `<a>` `<>` `<b>` `<c>` (any IFS char splits)
`IFS=""; v="a b c"; printf '<%s>\n' $v`  → `<a b c>`  (empty IFS = no splitting)
`v="a  b"; IFS=" "; printf '<%s>\n' $v`  → `<a>` `<>` `<b>`
`"$*"` joins with a literal SPACE regardless of IFS (observed with `IFS=,` → still space-joined).

=====================================================================
## 9. Interaction with globbing
=====================================================================

- Globbing happens only for LITERAL word text containing pattern chars:
  `cd /tmp/globtest` (contains g1, g2): `echo g*` → `g1 g2`.
- Expansion results are NEVER globbed:
  `x="g*"; echo $x`       → `g*`   (literal, even though g1/g2 exist)
  `echo $(echo "g*")`     → `g*`
  `x="*"; echo $x`        → `*`
- Glob with no matches: `nsh: error: no matches` on stderr, the word expands to nothing
  (observed via arithmetic-fallback cases), exit code remains 0.
- `**` in a glob pattern PANICS (see $((2**8)) in §5.2): pattern.rs:73
  `failed to glob: PatternError { pos: 0, msg: "recursive wildcards must form a single path component" }`
  (exit 0 when it happens inside a substitution subshell).

## 10. Exit-code / error-channel summary
=====================================================================

- Parse errors (bad `${...}` op, empty `x=`, unclosed `$((`, `$((x -= 2))` with spaces):
  stderr `nsh: parse error:  --> 1:COL` + caret context + `= expected ...`; exit 255; no stdout;
  nothing in the input executes.
- Unsupported-but-parseable `$((...))`: falls back to subshell command execution; diagnostics
  are runtime ones (`nsh: command not found \`NAME'`, `nsh: error: no matches`, panics in the
  child); the overall shell exit code stays 0 unless the LAST command's status says otherwise.
- Division by zero or i32-overflowing literal in VALID arithmetic, or `>(...)`:
  Rust panic on stderr (`nsh: panicked at ...` + backtrace + the "Something went wrong" trailer),
  exit 101, THE SHELL TERMINATES immediately (subsequent commands in the same input do not run).
- `~user`-family expansions: stderr warning `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported`,
  expansion continues as HOME, exit 0.
- `$?` is only ever the last command's exit status; failing command substitutions inside
  assignments always leave `$?` = 0.

part.text:
Spec written to `/workspace/specs/expansion.md` (501 lines, all behaviors verified by direct probing). Most important/surprising findings:

- **Field splitting is bizarre**: every unquoted expansion becomes its own field group, split away from adjacent literal text — `echo $HOME/x` prints `/tmp/nshprobe /x` (two fields), `pre${x}post` yields 3 fields, and empty/unset expansions yield ONE empty field (never removed). IFS splitting preserves empty fields with no collapsing (`" a  b "` → 5 fields).
- **Arithmetic is i32 with wrapping, right-associative chains**: `10-2-3` → 11, `100/10/2` → 20, `6/2*3` → 1 (but normal precedence otherwise). Supported: `+ - * / < <= > >= == !=`, unary `- +`, `=` (chained), and postfix `x++`/`x--` which return the NEW value (prefix semantics). Literals > i32::MAX panic (exit 101); division by zero panics and kills the shell (exit 101).
- **Unsupported arithmetic silently falls back to command substitution**: `$((10%3))` runs `(10%3)` as a subshell command → `nsh: command not found \`10%3'`, empty expansion, exit 0. Applies to `% ** << >> & | ^ ~ && || ! ?: , += ++x 0x.. base#n floats`.
- **Parameter ops**: only `-`, `:-`, `=`, `:=`, `${#V}`, `${V/pat/rep}`, `${V//pat/rep}` exist. The colon is a no-op (`${v:-d}` on empty-but-set v → empty). `:?`, `+`, `%`, `#`, `:offset`, `^`, `,`, `!` are all parse errors (`expected param_op`, exit 255) — there is no runtime "parameter unset" error at all.
- **Pattern-substitution replacement is not expanded**: `${x/l/$y}` silently returns x unchanged; `${x/#a/B}` anchors unsupported (no match).
- **Command substitution**: strips trailing newlines; in unquoted scalar (assignment) context the fields are joined with "" so `x=$(printf 'a\nb')` → `ab` (POSIX gives `a b`); double-quoted preserves interior newlines; `$?` after `x=$(false)` is always 0 (status never propagates). Backticks don't support `\`` nesting. `<(...)` works, `>(...)` panics exit 101.
- **Positional params only exist inside functions** — script args are rejected by clap (exit 1), `set --` is a clap builtin that errors, `source f args` ignores args. `$0`=script path in scripts, empty under `-c`. `$10` bare works as arg 10. Unquoted `$@` re-splits params on whitespace; `"$*"` always joins with a space regardless of IFS.
- **No magic variables**: RANDOM/SECONDS/LINENO/UID/PPID are unset plain vars; `cd` never updates PWD/OLDPWD; `$-` always empty; IFS starts unset but default space/tab/newline splitting still applies; expansion results are never globbed.
- **Tilde**: `~user`/`~+`/`~-` all print `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported` and expand to $HOME (cached at startup, survives `unset HOME`); tilde also expands after `=` mid-word (`a=~` → `a=/tmp/nshprobe`).
- **Empty assignment `x=` is a parse error** (exit 255, `expected ... or initializer`); must write `x=""`.
